claim: Restarts help only when the run-time distribution has a falling hazard (heavy tail or mixed easy/hard runs); they are neutral for exponential (Weibull k=1) and harmful for increasing-hazard shapes (k>1). No heavy tail was found for blocks-world planning (where randomisation gave only 30 min to 23 min), for local search (Walksat), for unsolvable instances, or for easy solvable instances.
agent_test: Log the finishing step of many independent attempts per task family. Fit the survival curve; if the share finishing per unit token falls over time, enable restart. Compare restart vs continue at equal tokens.
audit_note: Little or no gain was measured only for blocks-world (30 min vs 23 min); for local search, unsolvable and easy instances the sources report only absence of a heavy tail, and Gomes 2000 notes restarts are routinely used in local search.
claim_before_audit: Restarts help only when the run-time distribution has a falling hazard (heavy tail or mixed easy/hard runs). They are neutral for exponential and harmful for increasing-hazard shapes. Blocks-world planning, local search, unsolvable and easy instances showed no heavy tail and little or no gain.

claim: Randomised restarts with a small cutoff turned multi-hour or unsolved structured instances into minutes: logistics.d 108 min to 95 s; 3bit-adder-32 over 24 h to 165 s; 3bit-adder-31 over 24 h to 17 min; round-robin 14 411 s to 250 s; 16 over 24 h to 1.4 h; 18 over 48 h to 22 h (row mapping corrected, see critique). Blocks-world only 30 to 23 min.
agent_test: Re-run the same hard item set with and without fresh seeds plus a cutoff at equal total tokens; report solved count and tokens to first solve.
audit_note: Numbers match the corrected row mapping, but every usable source is the same Gomes/Selman/Kautz table (AAAI-98 Table 1 reprinted as Table IV in the 2000 JAR paper); Huang 2007 does not cover these instances, so it is one source.

claim: The best restart cutoff is far below the median run length and the cost curve is U-shaped. On logistics.d, cutoff 16 backtracks (success 0.009 per try) gave mean cost 1,861 vs 307,550 at cutoff 128,000. For an LLM search loop the best fixed cutoff was 12 to 24 iterations.
agent_test: Sweep attempt length (0.25x, 0.5x, 1x, 2x of a typical solved length) at fixed total tokens; plot solved share; look for an interior optimum.
audit_note: Minor: the 12 to 24 iteration cutoff comes from one LLM study on hot steel rolling and varies with the reward target.

claim: Luby's universal schedule needs no knowledge of the distribution and stays within a log factor of the best fixed cutoff. In practice it was best of seven policies in a clause-learning SAT solver (unit 32) and cost 1.1 to 1.8 times the best cutoff on an LLM search loop (unit 5); a unit that is too small (1) cost up to 2.8 times. Gap-search check: in Huang 2007 (251 instances, 2 h) Luby unit 32 solved 180 vs 178 for the best fixed cutoff (16000) and 174 for geometric (32,1.1), vs 127 with no restarts, so the Luby edge over a well-chosen fixed unit is small (d04).
agent_test: Luby schedule with unit near the measured typical attempt length vs fixed cutoff vs no restart, equal tokens, on tasks with checkable answers.
audit_note: Minor: 'best of seven' includes the no-restart baseline; the LLM-loop figures are simulated from one steel-rolling study.

claim: Dynamic restart policies that read early signals from the run (first 10 to 1,000 choice points) and set the cutoff from a learned predictor beat the best fixed cutoff by 40 to 65 percent in solution time on the tested families, but need offline traces from the same family.
agent_test: Train a small predictor on the first N tokens of past attempts (length, tool errors, stated confidence) to predict success; use it to abort. Compare with Luby at equal tokens on held-out items.

claim: With mixed run-time distributions and no per-run observation, the best fixed cutoff can be no cutoff at all, and a cutoff below the hard class's finishing time gives a finite chance of never solving it. Mixed task difficulty argues against one short cutoff.
agent_test: Run restart-heavy and continue-heavy arms separately on easy and hard strata; check whether one cutoff hurts the hard stratum.

claim: A portfolio of copies or variants run in parallel can beat the best single algorithm, and many copies of the better stochastic algorithm can beat a mixed portfolio. In an LLM search loop a K=4 portfolio of heuristics captured about 90 percent of the oracle gain (60.9 vs 65.1) and held on a held-out half.
agent_test: Keep the pool of candidates from restarts; pick K=2 to 4 with a cheap verifier on a validation slice; test on held-out items vs best single candidate.

claim: Parallel speed-up of independent restarts is predicted by the order statistic (minimum) of the sequential run-time distribution; an exponential gives linear speed-up. Shown on local-search CSP solvers up to 256 cores.
agent_test: Not directly testable on one sequential agent; use the maths to predict the gain of k parallel attempts from the measured one-attempt distribution.

claim: Independent resampling is a restart strategy for LLMs. With an automatic verifier, coverage grows roughly log-linearly with samples over four orders of magnitude (SWE-bench Lite 15.9 to 56 percent at 250 samples; MATH Llama-3-8B 82.9 percent at 100 samples to 98.44 at 10,000; CodeContests Gemma-2B 0.02 to 7.1 percent).
agent_test: Report coverage (any attempt verified) vs tokens for 1, 2, 4, 8 fresh attempts per item with a code or tool verifier; fit slope per task family.

claim: Choosing the right sample is the bottleneck: majority vote and reward-model selection plateau (MATH Llama-3-8B 40.50 to 41.41 percent from 100 to 10,000 samples) while coverage keeps rising; more calls with vote can even fall for hard queries.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare majority vote, LLM judge and code or tool verifier over N fresh attempts. Expect gains to track verifier quality, not N.

claim: Whether to continue one answer or restart depends on difficulty and task. Sequential revision wins on easy items, parallel or tree search on hard (Snell, trained revision model); backtracking beats parallel on Sudoku but loses on CountDown; ParaThinker and Hassid favour parallel short chains; one snippet-only report claims sequential wins. No rule holds across studies. Gap-search update: with all tokens counted, sequential refinement stays on the Pareto frontier and parallel drafts help latency only (d08); with Wait-extension and no check, parallel wins (d11, d12). The deciding factor is whether the continuation contains a real check.
schema_part: restart vs refine selection by difficulty
agent_test: Stratify items by first-attempt outcome or difficulty; at equal tokens compare continue, restart, and hybrid (one revision then fresh start) per stratum.

claim: Continuing from one's own earlier answer with a self-critique prompt and no outside signal does not help and often hurts (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8). Corrections work when an oracle label, tool result or test is supplied. Conversations that take a wrong turn rarely recover, and always-on reflection in an agent gave no overall gain. Gap-search update: unit-test feedback plus a self-written explanation also fails to beat resampling at small budgets (GPT-4 APPS 1.05x at 10 drafts + 1 repair, 0.97x at 2 drafts + 10 repairs); only a stronger critic or human feedback clearly helps (33.3 to 52.6 percent repair success) (d02, d03).
schema_part: G no self-judge as sole signal / refine operator
agent_test: Arm A refine with self-critique only; arm B refine with external check result; arm C fresh restart. Equal tokens, same items.
audit_note: Minor: the Huang GPT-4 GSM8K 89.0 and CSQA 41.8 figures are after round 2 (5 calls) of intrinsic self-correction; reflection result is from one agent benchmark.

claim: In reasoning models a long single chain locks in early mistakes. Within one question shorter chains are more often right, and several shorter independent paths beat one long path at the same tokens. Stopping at the first finished chains cuts compute (short-1@k up to 40 percent fewer thinking tokens).
agent_test: At equal total tokens: one long attempt vs k short attempts, with and without early stop at first finishers; reasoning model only.
audit_note: Minor: the parallel-vs-one-long-chain result is for the trained ParaThinker model, and the 40% saving is for one model (LN-Super-49B).

claim: The opposite failure also exists: reasoning models switch lines of thought too often. Wrong answers carry about 418 percent more thought switches and over 70 percent contain a correct thought; penalising switch tokens raised AIME24 pass@1 from 38.3 to 44.1 (QwQ-32B-Preview). Restarts should come at attempt boundaries, not mid-thought.
agent_test: Count switches in logged traces and check if wrong runs have more. Test a prompt rule that bans switching before a step is checked.

claim: Forcing a model to continue ('Wait') gives small gains that flatten (s1-32B AIME24 50.0 to 53.3 with two Waits and 56.7 with the main budget-forcing setting; MATH500 fell from 93.0 to 90.2 when the stop token was ignored with no string) and longer reasoning is not always better (GPT-4o on NaturalPlan peaks at a medium budget; R1 easy items 0.95 with short vs 0.72 with long traces).
agent_test: Compare stop-when-verified vs forced extra rounds at equal tokens; plot accuracy against rounds to find the flat point.
audit_note: In s1 the 57.6 is GPQA Diamond with no extrapolation; AIME24 is 50.0 without Wait, 53.3 with two Waits in the ablation table, and 56.7 (about 57) in the main result and the appendix 4-Wait row.
claim_before_audit: Forcing a model to continue ('Wait') gives small gains that flatten (s1-32B AIME24 50.0 to 57.6 with two Waits; MATH500 fell when the stop token was ignored) and longer reasoning is not always better (GPT-4o on NaturalPlan peaks at a medium budget; R1 easy items 0.95 with short vs 0.72 with long traces). Note from the s1 appendix table: AIME24 is 50.0, 53.3, 53.3, 56.7 for 0, 1, 2, 4 Waits (d13), so '57.6 with two Waits' above may be a different run; each AIME point step is one item of 30.

claim: Making the remaining budget visible to an agent lets a small budget match a larger one: Gemini-2.5-Pro BrowseComp 12.8 percent at budget 10 with tracker vs 12.6 at budget 100 without, with 40.4 percent fewer search calls. Plain ReAct saturates and does not use extra budget. Counter-evidence: a visible budget set too small can raise token use (token elasticity, d17), so the effect is not monotone.
agent_test: Add a budget line (tokens or attempts left) to each prompt; compare with no display at equal total tokens.

claim: A self-verifier that, after each attempt, returns SUCCESS, CONTINUE or PIVOT (pivot replaces the trajectory by a summary of findings) roughly doubled BrowseComp accuracy (12.6 to 24.6 percent). The decision is model-made, which conflicts with the schema rule that code, not the model, decides when to stop.
schema_part: restart with summary / G code decides
agent_test: Replace the model verifier by code rules (no new evidence for N steps, repeated tool error) and compare with the LLM verifier at equal tokens.

claim: In an LLM search loop (52 runs, steel rolling, Gemini 2.5 Pro) runs of 10 to 20 iterations match the hindsight-optimal split of a fixed budget; 5-iteration runs trail by 1.5 to 3.3 points and 30-iteration runs by 0.8 to 2.4. One-iteration sampling falls far behind.
agent_test: Replicate on a second domain: run 40 attempts, bootstrap the best split of a fixed budget into attempt lengths.

claim: Restarts add depth as well as breadth: in 14 of 15 Luby sub-runs the best result came from iteration 3 to 9 of the sub-run, not the first. A restart should leave room for several refinement rounds inside each attempt.
agent_test: Log in which round inside each attempt the best answer appears; if the first round dominates, shorten attempts.

claim: Carrying material across restarts is mixed. In clause-learning SAT, learned clauses persist and are part of why restarts work; in the LLM loop, seeding top-3 heuristics lowered the best (48.3 vs 51.6) but raised the median (43.2 vs 34.4), one campaign each, so noise cannot be excluded. Gap-search update: CSP evidence shows plain restart can cost (MAC+restart dom/ddeg 378 timeouts vs 365) while restart plus recorded nogoods wins (337) (d06); carrying wrong candidates into a PDR summary sharply lowers accuracy (d09); carrying the prior answer to a reasoning model gives +1 to 4 points but without an equal-token control (d10). Working rule: carry verified negative facts, not unverified answers.
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens: fresh restart, restart with a short verified-facts note, restart with prior best answer shown. Several campaigns each.

claim: Anytime LLM reasoning: answer quality after truncating the chain at a budget can be raised by prompting with good and bad truncated traces (PDP; final accuracy +17.6 percent over LEAP for strong reasoning models) or by RL (AnytimeReasoner, abstract only). Two-threshold stopping rules calibrated on 50 validation samples keep error under target.
agent_test: Force a final answer at 25, 50, 75, 100 percent of budget and score each; compare plain prompt vs contrastive-example prompt.

claim: Modern CDCL solvers restart very often (most restarts before the 1000th conflict), so restart changed from 'go elsewhere' to 'reorder what is already learned'. Clause learning with unlimited restarts simulates general resolution.
agent_test: Analogy only; test through the memory-carry arms in K20.
audit_note: Minor: the general-resolution result is from Beame et al. 2004, cited by Huang, not proved there.

claim: Foundations status after gap search: Huang 2007 tables and the Luby sequence definition and theorem statement were read from the primary PDF (d04, d05). Zilberstein 1996 is abstract only (the publisher PDF returned an empty body), Dean and Boddy 1988, Korf 1985, Luby 1993 and Huberman 1997 are still unopened. The anytime property list in the schema text is from memory.
agent_test: Open the primary papers before relying on property lists; then check monotone quality and interruptibility against our attempt logs.

claim: For a fixed item, repeated attempts behave like a constant per-attempt success chance (failure falls exponentially with the number of attempts). The heavy tail lives in the spread of per-item pass@1 across items, which makes the aggregate curve a power law. So restart-versus-continue gains come from item heterogeneity, and the within-attempt token hazard is still unmeasured. A model with no low-pass@1 tail (Llama 3 8B IT in jailbreaking) showed no aggregate power law.
agent_test: For 30+ attempts on each of 20 items per family, log tokens-to-correct. Fit per-item geometric rates and the hazard over tokens inside an attempt. Restart only on families where the within-attempt hazard falls.

claim: Within one attempt the chance of ending correct falls as the attempt gets longer: correct solutions are often shorter than wrong ones for the same question, and sampling until a short generation shows accuracy falling as the allowed length rises. This is indirect evidence for a falling hazard of success per token, the condition under which restart pays.
agent_test: Plot P(correct | attempt length bucket) on our items. If it falls past the typical solved length, set that length as the soft cutoff.

claim: Restart without memory can be a net cost, and restart with a small recorded set of verified failures recovers it. In a CSP solver plain restart raised timeouts from 365 to 378 (dom/ddeg) and from 277 to 298 (brelaz) and avg time from 125.0 to 159.0 s, while adding nogoods gave 337 timeouts and 109.1 s. With dom/wdeg failure weights restart already helped (140 to 123 timeouts).
schema_part: restart operator / what crosses a restart
agent_test: A/B: fresh restart vs restart plus a note listing only code-verified failed approaches and error tags, equal tokens.

claim: Carrying unverified material across a restart can anchor the next attempt: in Parallel-Distill-Refine, summaries from only-wrong drafts sharply cut accuracy, summaries from only-correct drafts raised it, and the drop was larger for the weaker self-verifier. Passing the prior answer to a strong reasoning model gave small gains (AIME24 80.3 to 82.1, 79.7 to 82.0) but at twice the tokens and with no equal-token fresh-sample control.
schema_part: restart operator / what crosses a restart
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens on ARC/BrainTeaser: no carry-over, verified-facts note, prior best answer. Count how often the next answer equals the carried one when the carried one was wrong.

claim: Answer-agreement stopping is a validated code-only stop signal for how many attempts to run: Adaptive-Consistency cut samples up to 7.9x with under 0.1 percent average accuracy drop (17 datasets, 3 models); ESC cut samples 33.8 percent (MATH) to 84.2 percent (Coin Flip) at comparable accuracy; DeepConf's consensus stop saved 52.8 percent of tokens at no accuracy loss (threshold 0.95). More aggressive thresholds (0.90) cost accuracy.
agent_test: Stop when the same code-checked answer appears in 2 of the first 3 attempts; compare tokens and accuracy with a fixed attempt count on ARC items.
audit_note: Minor: DeepConf 52.8 percent saving is one setting (DeepConf-low, AIME24, budget 512), and the 0.90 accuracy cost there is only 0.26 points.

claim: An LLM analogue of early-signal prediction exists: a sliding-window confidence signal (2,048-token window, threshold from 16 warm-up traces) aborts weak traces and cut tokens 43 to 79 percent versus majority voting at about equal accuracy on four math sets and five models. Overconfident wrong traces defeat it, it needs log-probabilities, and it was never tested at the first few hundred tokens or against Luby at equal tokens.
agent_test: Where logprobs exist, log windowed confidence of the first 500 tokens and test whether it predicts final correctness (AUC) on 30+ attempts per item.

claim: Under equal TOTAL tokens, refining one candidate with a re-check is on the Pareto frontier and parallel drafts mainly buy latency (o3-mini at 49k effective tokens: long CoT 76.9, sequential refinement 81.5, PDR 86.7 at matched sequential budget only). Under Wait-extension without a check, several short independent paths win (about 22 percent relative at a 16K budget). Net: restart is not a free lunch at equal tokens; it pays when the attempt has no check or the hazard falls.
agent_test: Equal-total-token arms on ARC and BrainTeaser: one long attempt, k=4 fresh short attempts, 4-round refinement with a code check, Luby unit-sized attempts.

claim: Showing the model its budget is not monotone safe: with a prompt-stated token budget that is too small the model overshoots and uses more tokens than with a larger budget (token elasticity); on the positive side an agent tracker lowered cost 31.3 percent at the same accuracy (K16). No study tests whether an attempt counter makes an agent quit early when combined with restarts.
agent_test: Two arms: counter shown vs hidden, with restarts allowed. Track the share of items abandoned before the first code-checked failure.
